newsitem.title: UK: Genetics can make super-crops, experts tell EU.
newsitem.headline: Genetics can make super-crops, experts tell EU.

text.p: Genetic engineering can help create crops that need less fertiliser, can grow in salty soil, and resist drought, scientists will tell the European Commission this week.

Although many consumers are nervous about eating food that has been genetically manipulated, researchers from all over Europe will report on ways they think the technology can make farming more environmentally friendly.

The 130 laboratories that took part in the 50 million Ecu ($56 million) Project of Technological Priority (PTP) will on Friday present their final reports on the plant biotechnology project, started in 1993.
Among them is Brian Forde of the Institute of Arable Crop Research (IACR) in Rothamsted, England, whose team used their EU grant to try to create plants that need less fertiliser.
"What we want to do is make them more efficient at using fertilisers," Forde told Reuters in an interview.
"So we work on the genes that control the process of nitrate uptake from the soil. We've isolated a new gene that controls this process."
Now the team is manipulating the gene to see if it can make the plant -- they are working with barley -- more efficient.
They want to create plants that "overexpress" the gene -- going into overdrive in making the protein that controls nitrate uptake.
Barley has 10 genes that regulate this process, which is probably why it was one of the earliest crops grown by humans -- it grows easily in varying conditions.
Crops more desired by modern society such as soybeans only have one or two genes, Forde said.
Inserting more genes should help a plant take up nitrates better. "I don't think you'd ever get away without using any fertiliser. Plants need a lot of nitrogen," Forde said.
"But the farmer would have to use less nitrogen."

Michel Caboche and colleagues at France's National Institute for Agricultural Research (INRA) at working to similar ends. They are reporting on work with the common fungus Aspergillus to find the gene responsible for transporting nitrates.

Roman Serrano of the Polytechnic University in Valencia and the IACR's Roger Leigh have found a gene in yeast that helps it live in an unusually salty environment. They have inserted the gene into barley, tomatoes and melons and found it helps them live in saltier conditions, too.
Dominique de Vienne and colleagues at the University of Paris coordinated an international effort that has found at least four different genes in maize that confer resistance to drought.
They hope these genes could perhaps be multiplied in the plants to create corn that could survive droughts.
Other teams are reporting on work in using genetic engineering to add vitamins to tomatoes and peppers and to stop crops such as wheat from wasting energy by growing taller than necessary.

Traditional plant breeding has created crops with some of these characteristics, but plant geneticists say manipulating genes can get stronger results -- and much faster. ($ = 0.894 European Currency Unit ECUs)
